title: The Lesson I Learned From Lazarus’ Grave
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Lazarus’ Grave
The Place Where I Thought God Was Late… Was Actually Where He Was About to Reveal His Glory
Have you ever stood beside something that felt dead and wondered why God never showed up?
A prayer you prayed for years.
A marriage that slowly fell apart.
A dream that collapsed without warning.
A child who walked away from God.
A heart that kept breaking in silence while everyone else thought you were doing fine.
Maybe you never said it out loud, but somewhere deep inside, you whispered the same words Martha spoke nearly two thousand years ago:
“Lord, if You had been here…”
Those words still echo through hospital rooms, funeral homes, broken homes, lonely apartments, and sleepless nights.
“Lord, if You had been here…”
If You had answered sooner.
If You had healed sooner.
If You had intervened sooner.
If You had stopped this before it happened.
The story of Lazarus is not merely a story about resurrection.
It is a story about every believer who has ever struggled with the painful silence of God.
It is a story about what happens when heaven seems late.
It is a story about the scandal of waiting.
And ultimately, it is a story about grace.
The Gospel of John tells us that Lazarus became seriously ill. His sisters, Martha and Mary, immediately sent word to Jesus.
They believed exactly what many of us believe.
If Jesus came quickly, everything would be okay.
But then something unexpected happened.
Jesus stayed where He was.
The text says:
"So, when He heard that Lazarus was ill, He stayed two days longer in the place where He was." (John 11:6)
At first glance, it feels almost offensive.
The One who loved them delayed.
The One who could heal waited.
The One who had power did nothing.
At least that is how it looked from earth.
Many believers secretly struggle with this reality.
We celebrate God's answers.
We praise His miracles.
We share testimonies.
But very few people talk honestly about the season between the prayer and the answer.
The waiting room of faith.
The graveyard of expectations.
The uncomfortable place where God appears silent.
Yet Scripture reveals something remarkable.
Jesus was never absent.
He was never unconcerned.
He was never late.
The Greek text uses the word δόξα (doxa), meaning glory, honor, divine majesty.
Jesus declared:
“This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God...” (John 11:4)
What looked like abandonment was actually preparation for glory.
What looked like delay was divine timing.
What looked like death was setting the stage for resurrection.
And suddenly the story begins sounding painfully familiar.
Because many of us have mistaken God's delay for God's absence.
We assumed heaven forgot.
We assumed God moved on.
We assumed our story was over.
But God was writing a chapter we could not yet see.
When Jesus finally arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days.
Four days.
Not four minutes.
Not four hours.
Four days.
In Jewish understanding, death was beyond question at that point.
Hope was gone.
The funeral was over.
The mourners had accepted reality.
The stone had already been rolled into place.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You have situations in your life that have been buried for years.
Dreams buried.
Relationships buried.
Opportunities buried.
Faith buried.
Hope buried.
You stopped expecting God to move because the stone has been there too long.
Martha met Jesus and said:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” (John 11:21)
That sentence carries the weight of disappointment.
It carries grief.
Confusion.
Questions.
Perhaps even frustration.
Yet Jesus did not rebuke her.
Because Jesus is not intimidated by honest pain.
He already knows what is in the human heart.
Then comes one of the most powerful declarations ever spoken.
In Greek:
Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
“I am the resurrection and the life.” (John 11:25)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say He knew where resurrection could be found.
He did not say He could perform resurrection.
He did not say resurrection was a future event.
He said He IS resurrection.
He IS life.
Not merely a giver of life.
Life itself.
Not merely a worker of miracles.
The source of every miracle.
The answer Martha needed was standing directly in front of her.
The answer many of us need is still standing before us today.
Jesus Himself.
Then something astonishing happens.
The shortest verse in the English Bible.
“Jesus wept.” (John 11:35)
In Greek:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
The Son of God knew Lazarus would rise.
He knew resurrection was minutes away.
He knew death would lose.
Yet He still wept.
Why?
Because God does not merely care about outcomes.
He cares about people.
He enters our pain.
He stands beside our graves.
He shares our tears.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
The God who created galaxies is also the God who notices broken hearts.
The God who commands resurrection also understands grief.
The God who conquers death also comforts mourners.
Then Jesus approached the tomb.
He gave a command:
“Take away the stone.”
Immediately Martha protested.
In the original text she essentially warns that decomposition has already begun.
The situation is beyond fixing.
The damage is done.
The smell confirms the reality.
How many times have we said the same thing?
Lord, it is too late.
Lord, this cannot be repaired.
Lord, this relationship is gone.
Lord, this addiction is too strong.
Lord, this person will never change.
Lord, my mistakes are too great.
But Jesus has a long history of stepping into impossible situations.
Then came the command that shook death itself.
“Lazarus, come out.”
And Lazarus emerged.
Still wrapped in grave clothes.
Still carrying evidence of where he had been.
But alive.
Completely alive.
The grave that was supposed to be his ending became a testimony.
And that is when I learned the lesson from Lazarus' grave.
The miracle was never just about Lazarus.
The grave became a classroom.
A place of revelation.
A place where human hopelessness collided with divine power.
A place where God's glory became visible.
A place where scandal became grace.
Because that is exactly what Jesus does.
Throughout Scripture He specializes in rewriting stories.
Abraham was too old.
Sarah was barren.
Jacob was a deceiver.
Moses was a fugitive.
Rahab was a prostitute.
David was an adulterer.
Peter was a denier.
Paul was a persecutor.
Yet Jesus rewrote every story.
The enemy writes death.
Jesus writes resurrection.
The enemy writes shame.
Jesus writes redemption.
The enemy writes failure.
Jesus writes grace.
The enemy writes endings.
Jesus writes new beginnings.
This truth reaches its highest expression at the Cross.
When Jesus died, many believed the story was over.
The Messiah was buried.
The stone was sealed.
Hope appeared lost.
Yet the very grave that looked like defeat became the greatest victory in history.
Three days later the tomb was empty.
The resurrection of Lazarus pointed toward the resurrection of Christ.
And the resurrection of Christ points toward the hope available to every believer today.
The Gospel is not that good people earn salvation.
The Gospel is that dead people are made alive through Jesus Christ.
Scripture declares:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.” (Ephesians 2:8)
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace, undeserved favor, unearned kindness.
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Grace.
Not performance.
Grace.
Not perfection.
Grace.
Not religious achievement.
Grace through Christ alone.
Maybe you came to this article carrying your own grave.
Maybe something inside you feels dead.
Maybe you are waiting for an answer that has not arrived.
Maybe you are wondering whether God forgot you.
Lazarus' grave reminds us that God's delays are not God's denials.
When Jesus arrives, even death must obey.
The stone is not stronger than Christ.
The darkness is not stronger than Christ.
Your past is not stronger than Christ.
Your shame is not stronger than Christ.
Your addiction is not stronger than Christ.
Your failures are not stronger than Christ.
Your grave is not stronger than Christ.
And perhaps today, Jesus is standing before your situation saying exactly what He said then:
“Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?” (John 11:40)
If this message spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What grave are you trusting Jesus to speak life into?
Because sometimes the grave is not where God abandons the story.
Sometimes the grave is where He begins rewriting it.
The stone you are staring at today may become the testimony you speak about tomorrow.
